# Mutations and responses

Source: https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/building-apps/server-functions/mutations-and-responses.md

The Add to cart form on the product page posts to `addToCart`.
When the write succeeds, the browser should land on the cart with the new line in it.
When the quantity is not a whole number, the caller should get a 400 and a message it can show next to the field.
When the database is down, the caller should get an error, and that error must not contain the failing query.

A return value can carry the cart line.
It cannot carry a status, a `Location`, or the instruction to refresh the cart, so those go through the response helpers in `@solidjs/web`.
Most applications need [`redirect()`](#redirect-the-caller), [`reload()`](#request-revalidation), and `throw respond(...)` from [Handle thrown errors](#handle-thrown-errors); the envelope internals are for integrators.

Mutations stay on the default `POST` transport, which is origin-checked.
Declare `GET()` only for reads.

## Return a value with response metadata

`respond()` pairs a value with a status and headers:

```ts
// src/data/admin.ts
import { getRequestEvent, respond } from "@solidjs/web";

export async function createProduct(input: CreateProductInput) {
	"use server";

	const userId = getRequestEvent()?.locals.userId;
	if (!userId || !(await database.users.isAdmin(userId))) {
		throw respond({ error: "Forbidden" }, { status: 403 });
	}

	const product = await database.products.create(input);
	return respond(product, {
		status: 201,
		headers: { "x-created-product": product.id },
	});
}
```

Call `createProduct(input)` from the admin page and the promise resolves to `product`, not to the envelope.
`respond<T>()` is typed as `T`, so the function's inferred return type is the product's, and a direct call made on the server during SSR unwraps the envelope the same way.
The transport applies the 201 and the header to the HTTP response.
A plain HTTP caller such as `curl` receives a JSON body with the same product in it when JSON carries the value faithfully; a value JSON cannot represent, such as a `bigint`, is encoded the same way as a plain return.

:::deep-dive[The envelope on the wire]
At runtime `respond()` returns a `ResponseEnvelope`, a `Response` subclass that carries the status, headers, and body, plus the `value` the caller should see.
Because it is a real `Response`, a fetch-style handler with no Solid knowledge can answer with it as it is.
The server-function handler forwards the response's status and headers and encodes the value as the body.
Integration code that has to recognize an envelope, such as a router applying revalidation, uses [`isResponseEnvelope()`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-web/request-response/respond); the check is a registered symbol, so it works when a bundle contains two copies of the runtime.
Application code never touches the envelope directly.
:::

## Redirect the caller

`redirect()` returns a `Response` with a `Location` header.
Its return type defaults to `never`, so a returned redirect drops out of the function's inferred return type; `reload()` is typed the same way:

```ts
// src/data/account.ts
import { getRequestEvent, redirect } from "@solidjs/web";

export async function deleteAccount() {
	"use server";

	const event = getRequestEvent();
	const userId = event?.locals.userId;
	if (!userId) throw redirect("/sign-in");

	await database.users.remove(userId);
	return redirect("/goodbye", { revalidate: "session" });
}
```

Return a redirect when it is the successful outcome, and throw it when it is an early exit, as in the sign-in check above.
Both reach the caller the same way.

What the browser does next depends on who made the call.
A Solid Router `action()` navigates to `/goodbye` without a page load.
An HTML form post without JavaScript is answered with the redirect itself, 302 by default, and the browser follows it.
Plain code that called `deleteAccount()` directly receives the `Response` object as the resolved value, because the transport hands navigation metadata back whole for the caller to apply.

The target can be a string or an `Href` produced by a router's typed paths helper; a branded `Href` redirects to its logical path.
Any other object throws `redirect() expects a string URL or an Href-branded value`.

## Request revalidation

`reload()` returns a response that tells an integration which cached reads are stale:

```ts
// src/data/cart.ts
import { reload } from "@solidjs/web";

export async function addToCart(productId: string, quantity: number) {
	"use server";

	await database.cart.add(currentSessionId(), productId, quantity);
	return reload({ revalidate: "cart" });
}
```

Call `addToCart("mug", 1)` through a router action and the cart query refetches when the call settles; nothing else on the page is touched.
Omit `revalidate` to ask for every cached read to refresh.

Core carries the keys in an `X-Revalidate` header and does not define a cache.
Solid Router reads the header against its query cache; [What revalidates after a mutation](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/routing/solid-router/data#what-revalidates-after-a-mutation) explains the matching.
`respond()` and `redirect()` accept the same `revalidate` option, for a mutation that also returns a value or changes location.

## Handle thrown errors

A returned or thrown `Response` or envelope is control flow, and the handler preserves its status, headers, and value.
A plain thrown value is treated as an accident:

```ts
// Avoid: a plain Error carries whatever message the failure had
export async function addToCart(productId: string, quantity: number) {
	"use server";
	if (!Number.isInteger(quantity) || quantity < 1) {
		throw new Error("Quantity must be a whole number");
	}
	await database.cart.add(currentSessionId(), productId, quantity);
	return reload({ revalidate: "cart" });
}

// Prefer: a response envelope for a failure the caller should see
export async function addToCart(productId: string, quantity: number) {
	"use server";
	if (!Number.isInteger(quantity) || quantity < 1) {
		throw respond(
			{ field: "quantity", message: "Quantity must be a whole number" },
			{ status: 400 }
		);
	}
	await database.cart.add(currentSessionId(), productId, quantity);
	return reload({ revalidate: "cart" });
}
```

In development the `Avoid` version rejects with the message as written.
In production the same call rejects with `Error("Internal Server Error")`: the handler replaces every unbranded thrown value before serializing it, so a database driver's failing query or connection string cannot reach the browser, and the quantity message goes with it.
The `Prefer` version rejects with `{ field, message }` and status 400 in every environment.

The line between the two behaviors is the build, not `NODE_ENV`.
`@solidjs/web` ships a development copy of the server-function handler behind the `development` export condition, which Vite's dev server resolves; every other resolution, including a production build and a plain Node process, sanitizes.

When the failure is an `Error` whose message is meant for the user, brand it instead of wrapping it:

```ts
import { markSafeError } from "@solidjs/web";

throw markSafeError(new Error("This coupon has expired"));
```

The brand lets the message and own properties cross the boundary in production.
Do not brand an error you did not construct: an error from a driver or a third-party client can carry anything in its properties.
Integration code can test the brand with [`isSafeError()`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-web/request-response/safe-errors).

:::pitfall[Returning a 400 makes the call succeed]
Only a thrown outcome rejects the caller.

```ts
// Avoid: returned, so the caller's promise resolves with the issues
return respond({ issues }, { status: 400 });

// Prefer: thrown, so the caller's promise rejects with the issues
throw respond({ issues }, { status: 400 });
```

With the `Avoid` version the HTTP response is a 400, and the promise in the browser resolves as if the write had worked; a router action records it as a successful submission with `{ issues }` as its result.
The status on a returned envelope is for HTTP callers; the throw is what tells the caller something failed.
:::

## Add router submissions

Solid Router's `action()` turns a server function into something a form can post to and the router can track:

```ts
// src/data/cart.ts
import { action } from "@solidjs/router";
import { reload } from "@solidjs/web";

export async function addToCart(form: FormData) {
	"use server";

	const productId = String(form.get("productId") ?? "");
	const quantity = Number(form.get("quantity") ?? 1);
	if (!Number.isInteger(quantity) || quantity < 1) {
		throw respond(
			{ field: "quantity", message: "Enter a whole number" },
			{ status: 400 }
		);
	}

	await database.cart.add(currentSessionId(), productId, quantity);
	return reload({ revalidate: "cart" });
}

export const addToCartAction = action(addToCart);
```

Render `<form method="post" action={addToCartAction}>` and the form posts to the function's URL before JavaScript loads; after hydration the router intercepts the submit, calls the function over the transport, and applies the `reload`.
The router marks the form `aria-busy` while it runs and, once it settles, records a submission whose `error` is the thrown envelope's value, which the [Forms guide](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/guides/forms) reads to show messages next to the fields.

Keep the server function a named export and wrap it separately, as above, so a test or an API route can call `addToCart` without the form.
When the function exists only for the form, write the body inline, `action(async (form: FormData) => { "use server"; ... })`; the [Data loading and mutations](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/routing/solid-router/data#mutate-with-actions) page uses that shape throughout, and the two behave the same.

:::note[Which action]
`action` here is from `@solidjs/router`.
`solid-js` also exports an [`action`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/lifecycle-actions/action), which runs a generator as a reactive transaction and has no URL; [Mutations](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/concepts/mutations) covers it.
A form needs the router's.
:::

When the router registers its single-flight integration, the mutation response can carry refreshed route data alongside the result; the server-function runtime treats that payload as opaque.

## Common problems

### The message is right in development and `Internal Server Error` in production

The function threw a plain `Error`, a string, or an object.
Production sanitizes every unbranded thrown value.
Throw `respond(value, { status })` for a structured failure, or `markSafeError(new Error(message))` for a message meant for the user.

### The 400 arrives as a successful result

The envelope was returned instead of thrown.
A returned envelope resolves the caller with its value whatever the status; `throw respond(...)` is what rejects.

### The redirect comes back as a `Response` object

The function was called directly rather than through a router action, and the transport hands responses that carry a `Location` or `X-Revalidate` header back whole.
Call the function through `action()`, or return a value and navigate in the caller.

### `redirect()` throws a `TypeError` about an Href-branded value

The first argument was an object that is not a string and not a router `Href`.
Pass a string path, or the value a router's typed paths helper returns.

## Recap

* Return a plain value when the caller needs data and nothing else; use `respond()` to add a status or headers to it.
* Return or throw `redirect(path)`; a router action navigates, a form post follows the redirect, and direct code receives the `Response`.
* Return `reload({ revalidate })` after a write so the router refetches the named reads.
* Throw `respond(value, { status })` for a failure the caller should see; a returned envelope resolves the caller whatever its status.
* A plain thrown value becomes `Internal Server Error` in production; `markSafeError()` opts one `Error` out of that.
* The development build is selected by the `development` export condition, not by `NODE_ENV`.
* Wrap a named server function with the router's `action()` for forms and submissions; write it inline only when nothing else calls it.

## Next steps

* [Progressive enhancement](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/building-apps/server-functions/progressive-enhancement): the same Add to cart form submitted before JavaScript loads, and what the runtime does with the 303.
* [Forms](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/guides/forms): the checkout address form, with the thrown 400 shown as inline field messages.
* [Metadata and transport](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/building-apps/server-functions/metadata-and-transport): attaching a header to every call and cancelling a call in flight.
* [Mutations](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/concepts/mutations): the client side of a mutation, with optimistic state and the reactive `action` from `solid-js`.

# Metadata and transport

Source: https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/building-apps/server-functions/metadata-and-transport.md

Open the network tab and click Add to cart.
The request is a `POST` to `/_server/data/<id>`, it carries `X-Server-Function-Instance` and `X-Server-Function-Format` headers the client runtime added, its body is the argument array, and the response leaves with `Cache-Control: no-store`.
Nothing on the product page asked for any of that; the transport has defaults, and most applications never change them.

This page is for the three cases where the defaults are not enough: every request needs a header that changes during the session, such as a bearer token; the endpoint has to live somewhere other than `/_server`; or one call needs to be cancelled while it is in flight.
Most applications need [Prepare every client request](#prepare-every-client-request) and [Configure one call](#configure-one-call).
Declaration metadata and invocation identity are for integrators and data layers.

## Attach declaration metadata

`withMeta()` attaches static metadata to a server-function reference:

```ts
// src/data/checkout.ts
import { withMeta } from "@solidjs/web/server-functions";

export const placeOrder = withMeta(
	async (cartId: string) => {
		"use server";
		return orders.place(cartId);
	},
	{ requiresAuth: true }
);
```

Nothing changes on the wire yet.
Metadata describes the function so that a `prepareRequest` hook or a data layer can read it; it runs no policy on its own:

```ts
// Avoid: metadata alone, expected to enforce something
export const placeOrder = withMeta(
	async (cartId: string) => {
		"use server";
		return orders.place(cartId);
	},
	{ requiresAuth: true }
);

// Prefer: the check in the body, metadata as the hint the client reads
export const placeOrder = withMeta(
	async (cartId: string) => {
		"use server";
		if (!getRequestEvent()?.locals.userId) throw redirect("/sign-in");
		return orders.place(cartId);
	},
	{ requiresAuth: true }
);
```

The `Avoid` version places any order for any caller; `requiresAuth` is a value on the reference, and the server never reads it.

Later `withMeta()` calls shallow-merge over earlier metadata.
`GET()` uses the same channel for its HTTP method, and the two compose in either order.
`live()` wraps the call behavior, so it goes outside both:

```ts
export const stockLevels = live(
	withMeta(
		GET(async function* () {
			"use server";
			yield* inventory.levels();
		}),
		{ channel: "inventory" }
	)
);
```

Integration code reads a declaration with `getServerFunctionMetadata(fn)` and checks that an unknown callable is a reference with `isServerFunction(fn)`.
Every reference exposes its stable `id` and its current `url`.

## Prepare every client request

`configureServerFunctionsClient()` configures the browser transport, and its `prepareRequest` hook runs before each fetch:

```ts
// src/entry-client.tsx
import { configureServerFunctionsClient } from "@solidjs/web/server-functions";

configureServerFunctionsClient({
	prepareRequest(init, { meta }) {
		if (!meta?.requiresAuth) return init;

		const headers = new Headers(init.headers);
		headers.set("authorization", `Bearer ${session.token()}`);
		return { ...init, headers };
	},
});
```

Click Add to cart again and the request to `placeOrder` carries an `authorization` header; a call to `getProduct`, which has no `requiresAuth` metadata, does not.
The hook receives the final `RequestInit` the transport is about to send, the function id, and the declaration metadata.

Use `prepareRequest` for policy that changes during a browser session: an OAuth token, a tracing header, a tenant id.
The configuration accepts one hook, so compose several policies inside one function.

:::caution[Call it before the first server function runs]
`configureServerFunctionsClient()` configures the transport for calls that have not started yet.
Call it once in the client entry, next to `hydrate()`, before any component that calls a server function renders.
:::

## Configure a custom endpoint

The default endpoint is `/_server`.
In start mode, the `serverFunctions.endpoint` option in `vite.config.ts` moves it, and the plugin configures the client and the server to match.

Configure the runtime directly only when you own both the client entry and the host:

```ts
configureServerFunctionsClient({
	endpoint: "/app/_server",
});
```

The client endpoint must be the path where the server mounts `handleServerFunctionRequest()`, base path included.
A mismatch shows up as 404s for every call, with nothing else wrong.

## Configure one call

`invoke()` calls a server-function reference with options that belong to one call:

```ts
// src/pages/checkout/Address.tsx
import { invoke } from "@solidjs/web/server-functions";
import { saveAddress } from "../../data/checkout";

const controller = new AbortController();

const result = invoke(
	saveAddress,
	{ signal: controller.signal, priority: "high" },
	{ name: "Ada", street: "1 Loop Road", postalCode: "12345" }
);

controller.abort();
await result;
```

The `await` rejects with the abort reason, and the browser cancels the request.

`invoke()` accepts three options:

* `signal` cancels the caller and the HTTP request.
* `keepalive` lets a small request continue while the page unloads.
* `priority` is a Fetch priority hint.

Build deadlines and combined cancellation with `AbortSignal.timeout()` and `AbortSignal.any()`.

Anything with a longer lifetime than one call is refused:

```ts
// Avoid: a header on one call
invoke(saveAddress, { headers: { authorization: token } }, address);

// Prefer: session policy in prepareRequest, static shape on the declaration
configureServerFunctionsClient({
	prepareRequest(init) {
		const headers = new Headers(init.headers);
		headers.set("authorization", token);
		return { ...init, headers };
	},
});
invoke(saveAddress, { signal }, address);
```

The `Avoid` version throws `` `headers` is not an invocation option `` with a pointer to where the option belongs.
Set headers in `prepareRequest`, declare reads with `GET()`, attach static values with `withMeta()`, and implement retries or deduplication in the data layer that owns the call.

:::note[Abort during server rendering]
During an in-process call on the server, an abort signal rejects the caller, and the underlying work runs to completion unless the function observes a signal of its own.
`keepalive` and `priority` have no effect there, because the direct call has no network request.
:::

Wrappers around a reference must forward the invocation channel for `invoke()` to reach it.
Application code normally uses the reference directly or through a data layer that already handles this composition.

:::advanced[Read the current invocation]
`getServerFunctionInvocation()` returns the identity of the server function that is executing, for logs and per-call cache keys:

```ts
import { getServerFunctionInvocation } from "@solidjs/web/server-functions";

export async function loadAccount() {
	"use server";

	const invocation = getServerFunctionInvocation();
	logger.info({ serverFunctionId: invocation?.id });
	return database.accounts.current();
}
```

Invocation identity describes the current call; `getServerFunctionMetadata(fn)` describes a declaration.
Use the first for logs and the second for transport policy.
:::

## Common problems

### Every call answers 404 after moving the endpoint

The client endpoint and the server mount point differ.
Set `serverFunctions.endpoint` in `vite.config.ts` so the plugin configures both, or check that `configureServerFunctionsClient({ endpoint })` names the exact path, base path included, where `handleServerFunctionRequest()` is mounted.

### `invoke()` throws that an option is not an invocation option

The options bag contained something other than `signal`, `keepalive`, or `priority`, such as `headers` or `method`.
Move headers to `prepareRequest`, the method to `GET()`, and static values to `withMeta()`.

### `invoke()` throws that the wrapper does not forward the invocation channel

The reference passed to `invoke()` is a wrapper, such as a cache or a channel, that shares calls between callers and did not opt in.
Invoke the underlying reference directly, or use the wrapper's own per-call options.

### The `authorization` header is missing on some calls

`prepareRequest` returned `init` unchanged for that call, or `configureServerFunctionsClient()` ran after those calls were made.
Check the condition in the hook against the metadata on the reference, and move the configuration to the client entry, before the first call.

## Recap

* The defaults are a `POST` to `/_server/data/<id>` with the argument array as the body and `Cache-Control: no-store` on the response; change them only for a reason on this page.
* Attach static facts to a declaration with `withMeta()`; the server does not read them, so enforce policy in the body.
* Compose `withMeta()` and `GET()` in either order, and put `live()` outside both.
* Add session-dependent headers in one `prepareRequest` hook, configured once in the client entry before the first call.
* Move the endpoint with the plugin's `serverFunctions.endpoint` option so client and server stay matched.
* Pass `signal`, `keepalive`, or `priority` to one call through `invoke()`; anything longer-lived is refused with a pointer to its home.
* On the server, an abort rejects the caller and does not stop the work.

## Next steps

* [Progressive enhancement](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/building-apps/server-functions/progressive-enhancement): the URL each server function exposes, and how a form posts to it before JavaScript loads.
* [Vite plugin server-function options](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/vite-plugin-solid/server-functions): the host-side configuration that pairs with the client settings on this page.
* [Deployment](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/building-apps/deployment): where a custom endpoint has to be routed when the app runs behind a provider.

# Progressive enhancement

Source: https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/building-apps/server-functions/progressive-enhancement.md

A shopper on a slow connection opens the product page and clicks Add to cart before the client bundle has arrived.
If the button's only wiring is an `onClick` handler, nothing happens, and the click is lost.
If the button is inside a form whose `action` is a URL, the browser posts the form, the server runs the function, and the shopper lands on the cart.

A server function has a URL, so the second version is available to every mutation on this cluster's pages.
The server-function runtime recognizes a browser form post at that URL, decodes the body as one `FormData` argument, and answers in a way the browser can follow with no script.

Application code reaches this through a router.
Solid Router's `action()` wraps the server function in a value that serializes to that URL, so the same `<form action={...}>` works before hydration and is taken over by the router after it.
Most applications need only the [router action](#post-a-form-through-a-router-action) section; the rest of the page is the transport underneath, for forms outside the router and for integrations that build their own form helpers.

## Post a form through a router action

Declare a server function that takes one `FormData` argument, and wrap it with `action` from `@solidjs/router`:

```ts
// src/data/cart.ts
import { redirect, respond } from "@solidjs/web";

export async function addToCart(form: FormData) {
	"use server";

	const productId = String(form.get("productId") ?? "");
	const quantity = Number(form.get("quantity") ?? 1);
	if (!productId || !Number.isInteger(quantity) || quantity < 1) {
		throw respond({ error: "Enter a whole number" }, { status: 400 });
	}

	await database.cart.add(currentSessionId(), productId, quantity);
	return redirect("/cart", { revalidate: "cart" });
}
```

```tsx
// src/pages/Product.tsx
import { action } from "@solidjs/router";
import { addToCart } from "../data/cart";

const addToCartAction = action(addToCart);

<form method="post" action={addToCartAction}>
	<input type="hidden" name="productId" value={props.id} />
	<input type="number" name="quantity" value="1" min="1" />
	<button type="submit">Add to cart</button>
</form>;
```

Load the page with JavaScript disabled and submit.
The browser posts to the function's URL, the server runs `addToCart`, and the redirect it answers sends the browser to `/cart`.
With JavaScript on, the router intercepts the submit, calls the function over the transport, and navigates to `/cart` without a page load.

The wiring that makes this work is the form, not the handler:

```tsx
// Avoid: the mutation exists only in a click handler
<button onClick={() => addToCart(new FormData(formElement))}>Add to cart</button>

// Prefer: a form whose action is the function's URL
<form method="post" action={addToCartAction}>
	<button type="submit">Add to cart</button>
</form>
```

Before hydration, the `Avoid` version has no handler attached, so the click does nothing; the `Prefer` version posts.

Everything the hydrated page does with a submission is a layer over that post.
Once the router is running it intercepts the submit, calls the same function over the server-function transport, sets `aria-busy` on the form while the call runs, records the result in `useSubmissions`, and runs any `.onSubmit` hook before the call is sent, which is where an [optimistic write](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/routing/solid-router/data#before-the-server-confirms) goes.
None of that changes the HTML or the server function, so a shopper whose bundle has not arrived gets the post and a fresh page, and a shopper whose bundle has arrived gets the same result painted before the server answers.

The [Forms guide](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/guides/forms) builds the checkout address form on this shape, with validation messages, pending state, and an address list that updates before the server confirms.

## Submit a GET form

A GET form replaces the action URL's query string with the form's fields.
When that query is not an encoded argument list, the handler passes it to the function as one `URLSearchParams` argument.

`GET()` returns a typed `ServerFunction` reference, so its `url` is available in TypeScript:

```ts
// src/data/search.ts
import { GET } from "@solidjs/web/server-functions";

export const searchProducts = GET(async (params: URLSearchParams) => {
	"use server";
	return database.products.search(String(params.get("q") ?? ""));
});
```

```tsx
<form method="get" action={searchProducts.url}>
	<input name="q" />
	<button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>
```

Type "mug" and submit: the browser navigates to `/_server/<id>?q=mug`, and the function receives `params.get("q") === "mug"`.

:::caution[A GET form describes a URL, not a mutation]
A `GET()` function must be safe and idempotent, because a `GET` request is not origin-checked and is replayed by caches, prefetchers, and link checkers.
Post mutations with `method="post"`.
:::

## The reference URL

Every server-function reference carries `id` and `url` at runtime, on the client stub and on the server-side callable alike.
`url` is the plain-HTTP address of the function, `<endpoint>/<id>`, and is what the router serializes into the form attribute.
The client runtime's own calls go to a sibling address, `<endpoint>/data/<id>`, so a cache never serves one caller kind the other's answer.

Whether TypeScript knows about `url` depends on how the function was declared:

* References returned by `GET()` and `live()` are typed as `ServerFunction`, which declares `id` and `url`.
* A bare `"use server"` function keeps its declared function type.
  `url` is present at runtime and absent from the type, so `addToCart.url` is a type error.

For a form post, use a router action rather than the URL.
An integration that must read the address from a bare declaration narrows it to `ServerFunction` from `@solidjs/web/server-functions` after checking `isServerFunction(fn)`.

## Bind leading arguments

The function id lives in the URL path.
An integration can add JSON-safe bound arguments in the reserved `args` query parameter, while the submitted form remains the final `FormData` argument.
Solid Router's `action.with(...)` does this for application code; with a `removeFromCart(productId: string, form: FormData)` action, the product id is bound and the form supplies the rest:

```tsx
<form method="post" action={removeFromCart.with(line.productId)}>
	<button>Remove</button>
</form>
```

`serverFunctionUrl(id, boundArgs)` builds that URL for a router, form helper, or custom host:

```ts
import { serverFunctionUrl } from "@solidjs/web/server-functions";

const address = serverFunctionUrl(removeFromCart.id, [line.productId]);
```

Bound arguments must be JSON-safe, because the no-JavaScript convention has no codec.
A `Date` or `Map` in `boundArgs` throws `Bound arguments in an action url must be JSON-safe`.

## Keep the checks in the function

A no-JavaScript submission reaches the same implementation as a scripted one, with the same `FormData`.
Validation and authorization inside the function cover both; a check in the component covers neither, because the component did not run.

:::deep-dive[What core owns and what the router owns]
Core owns the transport.
It decides by address whether a request came from the client runtime, decodes URL and form arguments, and provides the default `createNoJSHandler()` response for a browser form post: a 303 back to the page, with a non-`Response` outcome stored in a one-shot flash cookie.
It exposes `handleNoJS` so an integration can replace that policy, and it preserves response status, headers, bodies, redirects, and revalidation metadata on every path.

The router owns submission behavior.
It reads and clears the flash cookie during the next server render, turns the decoded outcome into submission state, and connects revalidation metadata to its query cache.

The core default applies when a custom host dispatches through `handleServerFunctionRequest()`.
A host can configure `createNoJSHandler()` with a base path or supply another `handleNoJS`; [server-function progressive-enhancement APIs](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-web/server-functions/progressive-enhancement) lists those hooks.
[Server rendering and hydration](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/routing/solid-router/server-rendering) covers the router setup.
:::

## Common problems

### `Property 'url' does not exist` on a server function

The function is a bare `"use server"` declaration, whose type is the function's own.
Pass it through the router's `action()` for a form, or, in integration code, narrow it to `ServerFunction` after `isServerFunction(fn)`.

### `Bound arguments in an action url must be JSON-safe`

A value bound with `.with()` or passed to `serverFunctionUrl()` was a `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, or another value JSON cannot carry.
Bind a string or number and convert inside the function, or pass the value through the form body.

### The form submits but the page reloads instead of staying put

The router is not mounted around the form, so nothing intercepts the submit and the browser follows the `action` URL as a full-page navigation.
The result is still correct, because the function ran and the redirect was followed; mount the form inside the `Router` to get the scripted path.

### The 400 shows nothing after a no-JavaScript submit

The outcome travelled back in the flash cookie, and something has to read it.
Solid Router reads the cookie on the next server render and records the submission; without the router, a custom host reads it through its own `handleNoJS`.
[Pass 3 of the Forms guide](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/guides/forms#pass-3-inline-errors-and-pending-state) shows the router reading it.

## Recap

* Put every mutation behind `<form method="post" action={...}>` so the browser can submit it before the client bundle runs.
* Wrap the server function with the router's `action()`; it serializes to the function's plain-HTTP URL and takes over after hydration.
* Pending state, `useSubmissions`, and `.onSubmit` optimistic writes are layers the hydrated page adds; the HTML and the server function stay the same.
* A browser form post follows a returned redirect; any other outcome is answered with a 303 back to the page and a flash cookie, which the router turns into a submission on the next render.
* Use `method="get"` and `fn.url` only for a `GET()` read; the function receives the fields as `URLSearchParams`.
* `url` is on every reference at runtime and only on `GET()` and `live()` references in the type.
* Bound arguments travel in the `args` query parameter and must be JSON-safe.
* Validate and authorize inside the function; a no-JavaScript request never ran the component.

## Next steps

* [Forms](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/guides/forms): the checkout address form, working before hydration and adding inline messages and an optimistic address list after it.
* [Data loading and mutations](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/routing/solid-router/data): what `action()` adds on top of this transport, including `.with()`, submissions, and revalidation.
* [Sessions and auth](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/building-apps/sessions-and-auth): the sign-in form, the most common no-JavaScript submission in a storefront.

# Streaming AI responses

Source: https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/building-apps/server-functions/streaming-ai-responses.md

The storefront gets a support assistant: a shopper types a question and the answer appears word by word as the model produces it.
Halfway through, the shopper asks a different question, or presses Stop, or the model call fails and they want to try again.
Written by hand, that is a `fetch` with a body reader, a flag for "streaming", an `AbortController` kept somewhere, and a text state that is replaced on every chunk.

In Solid the model call is a server function that returns an async generator, the browser side is a projection that writes one store commit per chunk, and cancellation is what the reactive graph does with a computation it no longer needs.
This guide builds that assistant and ends with the cancellation contract, because deciding who may stop a generation is the part that does not fall out of the code.

## Stream from the server

A `"use server"` function can be an async generator; the transport sends each yielded value over the open response as it is produced, as [Reads, streams, and live data](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/building-apps/server-functions/reads-and-live-data#return-a-stream) describes.
Read the request's abort signal and hand it to the model call:

```ts
// src/data/assistant.ts
import { getRequestEvent } from "@solidjs/web";

export async function* answer(question: string) {
	"use server";
	const signal = getRequestEvent()?.request.signal;
	const stream = await model.stream({ prompt: question, signal });
	for await (const chunk of stream) {
		yield chunk.text;
	}
}
```

`model.stream` is a stand-in for the provider SDK; provider SDKs take an `AbortSignal` for a streaming call under a name such as `signal` or `abortSignal`.
The parts that are Solid's are exact: [`getRequestEvent()`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-web/request-response/get-request-event) returns the request event on the server, and `request` is the standard `Request`, whose `signal` aborts when the client disconnects before the response has ended.

Call `answer("Do you ship to Portugal?")` from the browser and the first words arrive before the model has finished the sentence.
Each `yield` is one chunk on the wire; the function's `for await` loop is the only buffering there is.

:::caution[The signal is the host's to keep live]
`request.signal` fires on a dropped connection only when the server integration aborts it when the socket closes.
The Vite plugin's dev server does; a hand-written Node server must abort the controller on the response's `close` event, or the signal never fires and the model keeps generating for a reader that is gone.
:::

## Collect the chunks in a store

In the browser, [`createProjection`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/stores/create-projection) with an async generator turns the stream into a store.
Each `yield` commits the writes made to the draft since the previous one, so the component reads `reply.text` and sees it grow:

```tsx
// src/pages/Assistant.tsx
import { Errored, Show, createProjection, createSignal } from "solid-js";
import { invoke } from "@solidjs/web/server-functions";
import { answer } from "../data/assistant";

type Reply = { text: string; done: boolean };

function Assistant() {
	const [question, setQuestion] = createSignal("");
	let current: AbortController | undefined;

	const reply = createProjection(
		async function* (draft: Reply) {
			const asked = question();
			draft.text = "";
			draft.done = !asked;
			yield;
			if (!asked) return;

			const controller = (current = new AbortController());
			try {
				const chunks = await invoke(
					answer,
					{ signal: controller.signal },
					asked
				);
				for await (const chunk of chunks) {
					draft.text += chunk;
					yield;
				}
			} catch (error) {
				if (!controller.signal.aborted) throw error;
			}
			draft.done = true;
		},
		{ text: "", done: true },
		{ seedLoadingValue: true }
	);

	return (
		<>
			<form
				onSubmit={(event) => {
					event.preventDefault();
					const data = new FormData(event.currentTarget);
					setQuestion(String(data.get("question") ?? ""));
				}}
			>
				<input name="question" placeholder="Ask about an order" />
				<button type="submit">Ask</button>
				<button
					type="button"
					disabled={reply.done}
					onClick={() => current?.abort()}
				>
					Stop
				</button>
			</form>
			<Errored
				fallback={(error, reset) => (
					<p role="alert">
						{String(error())} <button onClick={reset}>Retry</button>
					</p>
				)}
			>
				<p>{reply.text}</p>
				<Show when={!reply.done}>
					<span aria-live="polite">Writing…</span>
				</Show>
			</Errored>
		</>
	);
}
```

Submit a question and the paragraph fills in chunk by chunk while "Writing…" shows; when the generator finishes, `done` flips and the indicator goes away.
Submit a second question while the first is still streaming and the text clears and starts again with the new answer; nothing from the first answer arrives afterwards.

What happens on that second submit is the whole cancellation story on the client side.
The projection's function read `question()`, so the new value re-runs it.
A re-run supersedes the previous flight: the runtime calls `return()` on the previous generator, which exits its `for await` loop, which in turn closes the server function's iterable and aborts the request.
Draft writes the old generator makes after that point are ignored, which is why a late chunk from the first answer cannot land in the second.

The `seedLoadingValue` option makes the seed, `{ text: "", done: true }`, the store's first committed value, so the first render shows an empty reply and no [`Loading`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/concepts/boundaries) boundary is needed above the paragraph.

### Two ways to stop

The second submit stops the first answer by superseding the read.
That is the shape to prefer: there is no controller to keep, and anything that re-runs the projection, including a `refresh(reply)`, cancels the same way.

The Stop button is the explicit form.
[`invoke()`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-web/server-functions/invoke) calls a server function reference with options that belong to one call, and `signal` is one of them: aborting it rejects the call and cancels the request.
The `catch` turns that rejection into a normal end when the abort was ours, so the text so far stays on screen and `done` flips; any other failure is rethrown.
Without the `catch`, Stop would be an error the boundary shows, which is not what the shopper asked for.

The controller lives in a plain variable rather than a signal on purpose: assigning it is not a reactive write, so the projection's function may do it, and nothing renders from it.

### Errors and retry

A rejected model call, a network failure after the first chunk, or an exception in the generator ends the projection's flight with an error, and the nearest [`Errored`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/components-jsx/errored) boundary renders its fallback.
The fallback's `reset` re-runs the sources that failed, so Retry asks the same question again with no state to clear by hand.

## Render Markdown without re-rendering the answer

A model answers in Markdown, and parsing the whole text on every chunk gets slower as the answer grows and rebuilds DOM the reader is looking at.
Split the answer into completed blocks and one trailing block: a completed block never changes, so it is parsed once and keyed; only the trailing block is re-rendered per chunk.

```tsx
// src/pages/Assistant.tsx
import { For, createProjection, createSignal } from "solid-js";
import { answer } from "../data/assistant";

type Block = { id: number; source: string };
type Reply = { blocks: Block[]; tail: string; done: boolean };

function Assistant() {
	const [question, setQuestion] = createSignal("");
	let nextId = 0;

	const reply = createProjection(
		async function* (draft: Reply) {
			const asked = question();
			draft.blocks = [];
			draft.tail = "";
			draft.done = !asked;
			yield;
			if (!asked) return;

			for await (const chunk of await answer(asked)) {
				draft.tail += chunk;
				const parts = draft.tail.split("\n\n");
				draft.tail = parts.pop() ?? "";
				for (const source of parts) draft.blocks.push({ id: nextId++, source });
				yield;
			}
			if (draft.tail) draft.blocks.push({ id: nextId++, source: draft.tail });
			draft.tail = "";
			draft.done = true;
		},
		{ blocks: [], tail: "", done: true },
		{ seedLoadingValue: true }
	);

	return (
		<article>
			<For each={reply.blocks} keyed={(block) => block.id}>
				{(block) => <div innerHTML={renderMarkdown(block().source)} />}
			</For>
			<div innerHTML={renderMarkdown(reply.tail)} />
		</article>
	);
}
```

`renderMarkdown` is a stand-in for the Markdown library of your choice; sanitize its output before using `innerHTML` on text a model produced.
A blank line closes a block, which is a good enough boundary for paragraphs, headings, and lists; a parser that reports where a block ends can replace the `split`.

Ask a long question and watch the DOM: each completed paragraph is inserted once and never touched again, and only the last `div` changes as chunks arrive.
`For` keyed by `id` keeps a block's element when the array is replaced, for example when the finished answer is written back from a saved conversation, and `push` on the draft adds a row without rebuilding the others.

## The cancellation contract

Three parties can stop a generation, and the code above connects them in one direction.
State the contract in the server function's comment, because a reader of either side cannot see the other:

1. The browser aborts: a superseding read, a Stop button, or a closed tab ends the iteration or the request.
2. The server's `request.signal` aborts, and the runtime calls `return()` on the generator, so its `finally` blocks run.
3. The generator forwarded that signal to the model call, so the provider stops generating.

Step 3 is the one the author decides.
A generator that does not pass the signal on still ends, but only at its next `yield`, after the model has produced one more chunk for nobody; a model call that runs to completion for a reader who left is the cost of forgetting it.

Forwarding is right for a chat answer, where the shopper is the only consumer and an abandoned answer has no value.
It is wrong for a durable job: a report the shopper asked to be generated into their account should finish whether or not they stay on the page, and reloading the page should show its progress rather than start it again.
Do not forward the signal to such a job.
Start it with an action, store its output on the server as it is produced, expose progress as a [live source](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/building-apps/server-functions/reads-and-live-data#declare-a-live-source) the page reads, and expose Stop as a second action that the job checks between steps.
In that shape the request's abort means only "this reader left", which is the correct meaning; the job's own lifetime belongs to the server.

:::note[What a superseded read cannot do]
Cancellation from the reactive graph stops the stream the component was reading.
It cannot stop work the server function started and did not tie to the signal, such as a job enqueued before the first `yield`.
If the function has side effects beyond the stream, give them the server-owned shape above.
:::

## Common problems

### The old answer's chunks appear after a new question

The generator reads the question after its first `await`, so the re-run tracked nothing and the first flight was never superseded.
Read every reactive input before the first `await` or `yield`, as `asked` is read above.

### Stop shows the error fallback

The abort's rejection reached the boundary.
Catch it in the generator and rethrow only when `controller.signal.aborted` is false.

### The model keeps running after the tab closes

`request.signal` never fired.
Check that the server integration aborts the request on a closed socket, and that the generator passes the signal to the model call rather than only reading it.

### The fallback flashes before the first chunk

The projection was read under a `Loading` boundary without `seedLoadingValue`, so the seed was not observable until the first `yield` landed, and the boundary showed its fallback for that window.
Pass `{ seedLoadingValue: true }` when the seed is a valid first render, or keep the boundary and accept the fallback.

## Recap

* Return an async generator from a `"use server"` function and pass `getRequestEvent()?.request.signal` to the model call.
* Consume the stream in `createProjection(async function* (draft) { ... })`; each `yield` commits the draft writes made since the last one.
* Read every reactive input before the first `await` so a change supersedes the flight, which closes the previous generator and aborts its request.
* Use `invoke(fn, { signal }, ...args)` for an explicit Stop, and catch the abort so the text so far stays on screen.
* Put completed Markdown blocks in a `For` keyed by `id` and re-render only the trailing block.
* Forward the signal when the reader is the only consumer; for a durable job, do not forward it, and expose Stop as an action.

* [Metadata and transport](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/building-apps/server-functions/metadata-and-transport#configure-one-call): the other per-call options `invoke()` accepts, and what it refuses.
* [Mutations](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/concepts/mutations): actions and optimistic stores, for the server-owned job shape.

# Durable generation

Source: https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/building-apps/server-functions/durable-generation.md

The support assistant from [Streaming AI responses](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/building-apps/server-functions/streaming-ai-responses) answers while the shopper watches, and stops when they leave.
That is the right contract for a quick question.
It is the wrong one for a summary of a forty-message order dispute: the shopper closes the tab to find the order number, comes back, and the summary starts over, because the request that was writing it ended with the tab.

The difference is who owns the generation.
In the streaming guide the request owns it, and the reactive graph cancels it.
On this page a job on the server owns it: an action starts the job and returns, the job writes the reply into storage as the model produces it, and every page that shows the reply reads what is stored through a live source.
Pick the request-scoped shape when the reader is the only consumer and an abandoned answer has no value; pick this shape when the reply must finish without its reader, be found again on reload, or be read from more than one tab.

Two deliveries are shown.
The client-owned one sends the reply as data through [`live()`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-web/server-functions/live) and renders it in the browser.
The server-owned one renders the whole thread on the server as a live server component, which is the shape of the `chat` example in the Solid repository; server components are an experimental preview, and that section says so.
The job, the storage, and the actions are the same in both.

## The job

Three modules carry the shape: a store the job writes into, a registry of running jobs that no request owns, and the actions that start and stop one.

The store keeps each reply and tells watchers when it changes:

```ts
// src/server/replies.ts
export type Reply = {
	id: string;
	text: string;
	status: "generating" | "complete" | "stopped" | "failed";
	error?: string;
};

const replies = new Map<string, Reply & { version: number }>();
const waiters = new Map<string, Set<() => void>>();

export function write(id: string, patch: Partial<Reply>) {
	const current = replies.get(id)!;
	replies.set(id, { ...current, ...patch, version: current.version + 1 });
	const waiting = waiters.get(id);
	waiters.delete(id);
	waiting?.forEach((wake) => wake());
}

function changed(id: string, signal?: AbortSignal) {
	return new Promise<void>((wake) => {
		(waiters.get(id) ?? waiters.set(id, new Set()).get(id)!).add(wake);
		signal?.addEventListener("abort", () => wake(), { once: true });
	});
}

// The reply as it stands now, then again after every write.
export async function* watch(id: string, signal?: AbortSignal) {
	let seen = -1;
	while (!signal?.aborted) {
		const current = replies.get(id);
		if (current && current.version !== seen) {
			seen = current.version;
			yield current as Reply;
			continue;
		}
		await changed(id, signal);
	}
}
```

`watch` checks the version after every yield before it waits, so a write that lands while the consumer holds the previous value is not missed.
The `chat` example keeps the same shape in `src/server/db.ts`, written through to disk so a reply survives a restart.

The job reads from the model and writes into the store.
It belongs to the module, not to a request:

```ts
// src/server/generations.ts
import * as replies from "./replies";

const running = new Map<string, AbortController>();

export function start(replyId: string, history: Message[]) {
	const abort = new AbortController();
	running.set(replyId, abort);
	void (async () => {
		let text = "";
		try {
			for await (const chunk of model.stream({
				history,
				signal: abort.signal,
			})) {
				text += chunk.text;
				replies.write(replyId, { text });
			}
			replies.write(replyId, { status: "complete" });
		} catch (error) {
			if (abort.signal.aborted) replies.write(replyId, { status: "stopped" });
			else
				replies.write(replyId, {
					status: "failed",
					error: "The model stopped answering",
				});
		} finally {
			running.delete(replyId);
		}
	})();
}

export function stop(replyId: string) {
	running.get(replyId)?.abort();
}
```

`model.stream` is a stand-in for the provider SDK, as in the streaming guide.
The signal it receives is the job's own, not a request's: Stop aborts it, and nothing else does.
A reply that fails keeps the text that had arrived, with the reason beside it; a reply that was stopped keeps its text and says so.
Write at most every few tens of milliseconds when the model is fast, as the example does, since every write wakes every watcher.

The actions start and stop a job and return at once:

```ts
// src/data/replies.ts
import { action } from "@solidjs/router";
import * as generations from "../server/generations";
import * as replies from "../server/replies";
import * as threads from "../server/threads";

export const sendMessage = action(
	async (threadId: string, messageId: string, text: string) => {
		"use server";
		const { replyId, history } = await threads.append(
			threadId,
			messageId,
			text
		);
		generations.start(replyId, history);
	},
	"sendMessage"
);

export const stopReply = action(async (replyId: string) => {
	"use server";
	generations.stop(replyId);
}, "stopReply");
```

`sendMessage` stores the shopper's message and an empty reply with status `generating`, starts the job, and returns.
The response closes while the job is still writing; the server-function runtime does not dispose work a function started, so the job runs to its end whether or not anyone is watching.
`threads.append` is the thread half of the store, which keeps the message list and the history the model reads; the `chat` example's `db.send` is one.
Both actions are Solid Router [actions](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/routing/solid-router/data#mutate-with-actions), so they work as a form before JavaScript has loaded and from code through `useAction`.

:::caution[An orphan is a fact, not a hang]
A server restart ends every running job and leaves the replies they were writing at `generating`.
Mark them `failed` with a reason when the store loads, as the `chat` example does, so a reader sees a message with a Retry rather than a reply that never finishes.
:::

## Client-owned: the browser renders the reply

The live source yields the reply so far, whole, on every write:

```ts
// src/data/replies.ts
import { getRequestEvent } from "@solidjs/web";
import { GET, live } from "@solidjs/web/server-functions";
import * as replies from "../server/replies";

export const watchReply = live(
	GET(async function* (replyId: string) {
		"use server";
		const signal = getRequestEvent()?.request.signal;
		for await (const reply of replies.watch(replyId, signal)) yield reply;
	})
);
```

The request's signal ends the watcher when the reader leaves; the job does not see it.
The first yield on every connection is the current reply, which is the contract `live()` reconnects on, as [Declare a live source](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/building-apps/server-functions/reads-and-live-data#declare-a-live-source) describes.

In the browser, [`createProjection`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/stores/create-projection) with an async generator turns the stream into a store:

```tsx
// src/pages/Reply.tsx
import { Show, createProjection } from "solid-js";
import { stopReply, watchReply } from "../data/replies";

type ReplyView = { text: string; status: string; error?: string };

function Reply(props: { replyId: string }) {
	const reply = createProjection(
		async function* (draft: ReplyView) {
			for await (const next of watchReply(props.replyId)) {
				draft.text = next.text;
				draft.status = next.status;
				draft.error = next.error;
				yield;
			}
		},
		{ text: "", status: "generating" },
		{ seedLoadingValue: true }
	);

	return (
		<article>
			<p>{reply.text}</p>
			<Show when={reply.status === "generating"}>
				<form action={stopReply.with(props.replyId)} method="post">
					<button type="submit">Stop</button>
				</form>
			</Show>
			<Show when={reply.status === "failed"}>
				<p role="alert">{reply.error}</p>
			</Show>
		</article>
	);
}
```

Send a message, close the tab while the reply is being written, and open the page again.
The component calls `watchReply` again, the first yield is the reply as far as it had got, and the paragraph keeps growing from there.
Open the page in two tabs and both show the same reply; press Stop in one and the status changes in both, because Stop aborted the job and the job wrote `stopped` into the store every watcher reads.

The projection reads `props.replyId` before its first `await`, so a different reply re-runs it, which ends the previous iteration and its connection.
A projection rather than a memo keeps readers of `reply.status` out of every text update, and gives the Markdown block split from [Render Markdown without re-rendering the answer](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/building-apps/server-functions/streaming-ai-responses#render-markdown-without-re-rendering-the-answer) a draft to write into.
`refresh(reply)` re-runs the projection, which opens a new connection; it does not touch the job.

Every call site that iterates a live source holds its own connection.
When the thread list and the thread both need the same reply, hoist the read, or declare it with Solid Router's [`liveQuery`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-router/data#livequery), which keeps one connection per key for every consumer; the spelling is `liveQuery(watchReply, "reply")`, and a function already declared with `live(GET())` passes through unchanged.

## Hold the bubble until the stream confirms

The shopper's own message should be on screen the moment they press Enter, and should give way to the server's row when the thread shows it.
The thread is read through a live source, so the confirmation arrives on the stream rather than in the action's response.
That is what [`until`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/lifecycle-actions/until) waits for:

```tsx
// src/components/Composer.tsx
import { For, action, createOptimisticStore, until } from "solid-js";
import { useAction } from "@solidjs/router";
import { sendMessage } from "../data/replies";

type Pending = { id: string; text: string };

function Composer(props: { threadId: string; seen: string[] }) {
	const send = useAction(sendMessage);
	const [outbox, setOutbox] = createOptimisticStore<Pending[]>([]);

	const submit = action(function* (text: string) {
		const id = crypto.randomUUID();
		setOutbox((list) => {
			list.push({ id, text });
		});
		yield send(props.threadId, id, text);
		yield until(() => props.seen.includes(id), { timeout: 15_000 });
	});

	return (
		<>
			<For each={outbox.filter((m) => !props.seen.includes(m.id))}>
				{(message) => <p class="pending">{message.text}</p>}
			</For>
			<form
				onSubmit={(event) => {
					event.preventDefault();
					const data = new FormData(event.currentTarget);
					void submit(String(data.get("text") ?? ""));
				}}
			>
				<textarea name="text" required />
				<button type="submit">Send</button>
			</form>
		</>
	);
}
```

`seen` is the list of message ids the live thread shows; the parent reads it from the thread's live source and passes it down.
The push onto `outbox` is an optimistic write: it shows at once and is held by the action's transaction.
`until` reads the authoritative `seen`, so the optimistic row cannot satisfy it; only the stream can.
When the row arrives, `until` resolves, the action settles, and the overlay drops.
A timeout or a server error rejects the action, which drops the overlay the same way and leaves the shopper's text to send again.

The `For` also filters the outbox by `seen`.
The action's overlay is released a task after the data that satisfied its `until` lands, so without the filter a frame can show the bubble and the row together; deriving the bubble's visibility from `seen` closes that gap, and `until` keeps its job of settling the action on failure and timeout.

`action` here is the one from `solid-js`, which runs a generator as one transaction; `sendMessage` is a Solid Router action, bound to the router with `useAction` so a call from code carries its revalidation and submission tracking.

## Server-owned: the thread as a live server component

:::caution[Server components are an experimental preview]
A function returned from a `"use server"` function is a server component, mounted in the browser with `dynamicComponent`.
The runtime ships in `@solidjs/web` and is excluded from Solid 2.0's stability guarantees: the API and the wire format may change between prereleases.
The `chat` example in the Solid repository is this section's reference implementation.
:::

When the markdown renderer, the highlighter, and the model client should stay on the server, the thread can be server markup that keeps changing.
The server function returns a component instead of data, and `live()` holds the response open while it re-renders:

```tsx
// src/routes/thread.tsx
import { createMemo, onCleanup } from "solid-js";
import { getRequestEvent } from "@solidjs/web";
import { GET, live } from "@solidjs/web/server-functions";
import type { Slot } from "@solidjs/web/frames";
import { liveQuery } from "@solidjs/router";
import { stopReply } from "../data/replies";
import * as threads from "../server/threads";

type ComposerSlot = Slot<{ threadId: string; seen: string[] }>;

export const getThread = liveQuery(
	live(
		GET(async (id: string) => {
			"use server";
			return (props: { composer: ComposerSlot }) => {
				const gone = new AbortController();
				onCleanup(() => gone.abort());
				getRequestEvent()?.request.signal.addEventListener("abort", () =>
					gone.abort()
				);
				const view = createMemo(() => threads.watch(id, gone.signal));
				return (
					<article>
						{view().messages.map((message) => (
							<section data-id={message.id}>
								<div innerHTML={renderMarkdown(message.text)} />
								{message.status === "generating" && (
									<form action={stopReply.with(message.id)} method="post">
										<button type="submit">Stop</button>
									</form>
								)}
							</section>
						))}
						<props.composer
							$key={id}
							threadId={id}
							seen={view().messages.map((m) => m.id)}
						/>
					</article>
				);
			};
		})
	),
	"thread"
);
```

`threads.watch` is the thread-level watcher: it yields the thread and its messages after every write to any of them.
The route component mounts the call and fills the slot:

```tsx
// src/routes/thread.tsx
import { Loading } from "solid-js";
import { dynamicComponent } from "@solidjs/web";
import type { RouteSectionProps } from "@solidjs/router";
import Composer from "../components/Composer";

export default function ThreadRoute(props: RouteSectionProps) {
	const Thread = dynamicComponent(() => getThread(String(props.params.id)));
	return (
		<Loading fallback={<p>Loading the conversation…</p>}>
			<Thread
				composer={(p) => <Composer threadId={p.threadId} seen={p.seen} />}
			/>
		</Loading>
	);
}
```

The composer from the previous section is the slot's fill: the server positions it at the foot of the thread and passes `seen` as a slot argument, so `until` reads the same ids the server rendered.
`$key={id}` makes a new composer per thread, so a half-typed message stays with its conversation.

What this shape adds over the client-owned one:

* The page's source carries the reply as far as it had got, because the document face renders the live source's first value, and hydration adopts it and connects.
* The browser bundle has no Markdown parser, no highlighter, and no model client.
* Every mutation is a form the server rendered, which works before JavaScript loads; a form that has been submitted stays marked busy while the markup around it changes.

What it costs: the server holds one render per open thread per tab, and the thread and the sidebar are two connections per tab, which is why the example serves HTTP/2 in development.

The example reads the thread through one watcher at the top of the render and cuts the markup into the finished messages and the reply being written, so a token re-sends the reply and nothing else.
A watcher created per message inside the list never settles, because each retry of the render makes a new one.

## Reconnect, and where a reply resumes from

`live()` reconnects a stream that dies after it has connected, with exponential backoff, and the first yield of the new connection replaces whatever the page shows.
Each event on the wire carries an id, and every reconnect sends the last id it received back as `Last-Event-ID`.
When that id equals the digest of the source's first yield, the server drops that yield: the client already holds it, so an unchanged reply costs nothing on reconnect.
For a live server component the reconnect also names the pieces of markup the page shows, and the server sends only the pieces whose digest differs.
After hydration, the first connection names the value the page was served with, so a server that still holds that value sends nothing.

What this does not do is replay the part of a reply between the last event and now.
The source yields the whole reply, so a reconnect gets the reply so far in one value, and a long reply costs its length each time.
Partial replay is a join with the job's log: keep an append-only log of chunks per reply, read the header in the source with `getRequestEvent()?.request.headers.get("last-event-id")`, and yield the chunks after that position.
A source that reads the header itself is a cursor source; the runtime's digest skip does not apply to it.
`@tanstack/ai-durable-stream` and Electric's Durable Streams are off-the-shelf logs of that kind, for a team that wants one rather than a table.

## Common problems

### The reply stops when the shopper leaves

The job received the request's signal instead of its own.
Give the job an `AbortController` the registry owns, and pass `request.signal` only to the watcher.

### Stop does nothing

The Stop action aborted a controller the job was not reading, or the job was started by a server that has since restarted.
Check that `generations.start` passes `abort.signal` to the model call, and that the store marks orphaned replies `failed` on load.

### Two tabs show different replies

Each tab is reading a copy the job made rather than the store.
The job writes once, into the store; every page reads the store through its watcher.

### The bubble and the server's row show together for a frame

The bubble leaves when the action settles, which is a task after the row landed.
Filter the outbox by `seen` as well as waiting on it with `until`.

### `Cannot call until inside a reactive scope`

`until` was called inside a memo or an effect.
Await it from an action body or another imperative scope.

## Recap

* Start the generation from an action that returns at once; the job belongs to a module-level registry and writes the reply into a store as it arrives.
* Pass the job its own abort signal; the request's signal ends only the watcher.
* Deliver the reply through `live(GET(async function*))`, yielding the whole reply so far and the current reply first on every connection.
* Render it in the browser with `createProjection`, or on the server as a live server component mounted with `dynamicComponent` through `liveQuery(live(GET(fn)), key)`.
* Hold an optimistic row with `createOptimisticStore` inside an `action`, confirm it with `until` over the live thread's ids, and filter the row by the same ids.
* A reconnect sends `Last-Event-ID`; an unchanged first value is skipped, and partial replay needs a log the source reads the header against.

* [Reads, streams, and live data](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/building-apps/server-functions/reads-and-live-data): `live()`, its reconnect, and `onstatus`.
* [Mutations](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/concepts/mutations): actions, optimistic stores, and `until`.
* [Data loading and mutations](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/routing/solid-router/data): Solid Router's `action`, `useAction`, and forms.
