# Solid for AI tools

Source: https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/guides/ai-tools.md

An assistant asked to add a feature to a Solid 2.0 app writes code from what it learned elsewhere: props destructured in the signature, an effect with one function, a store written through a path setter, `Suspense` and `createResource`.
Each of those is wrong in 2.0, and some of them run without an error, so the mistake shows up as a value that never updates rather than as a stack trace.

Solid 2.0 ships the material that corrects this, and most of it is installed with the packages so it matches the exact version in `node_modules`.
This page lists every piece, says what it is for, and ends with a block to paste into the assistant's instructions file.

## What ships with the packages

### The cheatsheet

`node_modules/solid-js/CHEATSHEET.md` is a one-page reference for Solid 2.0: imports, every primitive with a short example, and a section at the end titled "What changed from 1.x" that lists the renamed and removed names with their replacements.
Point an assistant at it before its first edit; the section at the end is written for a model whose training data is 1.x.

### Skills

A skill is a Markdown file an assistant reads on demand, placed under `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` inside the package that owns the behavior it describes.
Four ship with Solid 2.0:

| Path                                                            | Read it when                                                                                                                                                   |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `node_modules/solid-js/skills/solid-2.0/SKILL.md`               | Before the first edit. The primer: the run-once component model, where reads and writes may happen, and the shapes that replace 1.x APIs.                      |
| `node_modules/solid-js/skills/reactivity-diagnostics/SKILL.md`  | A diagnostic code such as `[REACTIVE_WRITE_IN_OWNED_SCOPE]` appears in the console or a test. One section per code: what the runtime observed, what to change. |
| `node_modules/@solidjs/diagnostics/skills/agent-loops/SKILL.md` | Verifying a reactive change: how to capture which scopes re-ran and why, and how to turn that into a budget a test asserts.                                    |
| `node_modules/@solidjs/web/skills/server-components/SKILL.md`   | Writing a `"use server"` component: where server markup ends, where a client slot begins, and the rules for binding the two.                                   |

The versions in `node_modules` match the installed runtime, which is why the paths above point there rather than at GitHub.
The same files are in the [solid repository](https://github.com/solidjs/solid/tree/next/packages) for reading in a browser.

### The template's AGENTS.md

Every project created with `pnpm create solid@latest` from a `solid-v2` template contains an `AGENTS.md` at its root.
It names the installed skills, explains the diagnostics endpoint, and tells the assistant to name its signals, memos, and effects so attribution reports read well.
Keep it; an assistant that supports the file reads it on every task.

## Diagnostics an assistant can read

A development build of Solid reports structural mistakes as coded console warnings, and the same findings are available as data in tests and over HTTP.
An assistant that works from evidence rather than from reading the code makes fewer wrong fixes, so each channel is listed here with how to reach it.

### Coded warnings with a repair-guide footer

In development, the runtime reports a structural mistake as a console diagnostic: a reactive value read outside a tracking scope, a write from inside a memo, an effect that re-runs because of its own write.
Each report carries a stable code in brackets, an `in` line naming the owners that enclose the subject, and an `at` line with the `file:line:col` the compiler recorded for it.
The first report of each code ends with a footer: a line for a person, linking the code's page in the [diagnostics reference](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/diagnostics), then a line for an assistant, naming the installed repair guide and the same file on GitHub, anchored to that code:

```
[REACTIVE_WRITE_IN_OWNED_SCOPE] what it means and how to fix it: https://v2.solidjs.com/reference/solid-js/diagnostics/reactive-write-in-owned-scope
[REACTIVE_WRITE_IN_OWNED_SCOPE] agent repair guide: node_modules/solid-js/skills/reactivity-diagnostics/SKILL.md#reactive_write_in_owned_scope — https://github.com/solidjs/solid/blob/next/packages/solid/skills/reactivity-diagnostics/SKILL.md#reactive_write_in_owned_scope
```

Tell the assistant to treat every code as a defect to look up in the guide, not as noise to suppress.
[Debugging reactivity](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/guides/debugging-reactivity) explains how to read a report, and the [diagnostics reference](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/diagnostics) has a page per code with the same repair written for a person.

### `DEV` and `OBSERVE`

[`DEV`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/advanced/diagnostics-dev-hooks/dev) is the development-only hook object exported from `solid-js`; it is `undefined` in a production build.
[`OBSERVE`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/advanced/diagnostics-dev-hooks/observe) is its counterpart in the observe build, which also carries the records and attribution channels that tooling subscribes to.
An assistant does not call these directly in app code; they are what the diagnostics package and the Vite plugin are built on, and they are listed here so an assistant that finds them in a stack trace knows what they are.

### `@solidjs/diagnostics` in tests

`captureArtifact` from `@solidjs/diagnostics` runs a scenario and returns a serializable artifact of every diagnostic and every re-run with its cause.
`expectNoDiagnostics(artifact)` throws with the offending events as evidence, and `expectRerunBudget` bounds how often a named scope may re-run.
The same checks are Vitest matchers, `toHaveNoDiagnostics` and `toStayWithinRerunBudget`, when the setup file imports `@solidjs/diagnostics/vitest`.

```ts
import {
	captureArtifact,
	expectNoDiagnostics,
	expectRerunBudget,
} from "@solidjs/diagnostics";

const { artifact } = await captureArtifact(
	() => {
		// mount a tree, perform the interaction under test
	},
	{ scenario: "cart-add" }
);

expectNoDiagnostics(artifact);
expectRerunBudget(artifact, 1, { scope: "total" });
```

An assistant can run this loop on its own: generate, capture, read the events, fix, capture again, until the artifact is empty.
[Check for regressions in tests](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/guides/debugging-reactivity#check-for-regressions-in-tests) shows the matcher form.

### The dev server endpoint

With `diagnostics: true` in the `@solidjs/vite-plugin` options, the dev server serves `/__solid/diagnostics`.
`GET` returns the status, including whether a page is connected.
`POST` with a JSON body `{"method": ...}` drives a capture session against the open page:

| Method      | Params                     | Result                                      |
| ----------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `begin`     | optional `{ attribution }` | opens a capture session                     |
| `end`       | none                       | closes it and returns the captured payload  |
| `active`    | none                       | whether a session is open                   |
| `whyDidRun` | `{ "name": "..." }`        | the recorded re-runs of one named scope     |
| `costs`     | none                       | the running cost tables of the open session |

```sh
curl -X POST localhost:3000/__solid/diagnostics -d '{"method":"begin"}'
# interact with the page in a browser
curl -X POST localhost:3000/__solid/diagnostics -d '{"method":"whyDidRun","params":{"name":"CartTotal"}}'
curl -X POST localhost:3000/__solid/diagnostics -d '{"method":"end"}'
```

Scopes are reported by name, so an assistant that names its memos and effects with the `{ name }` option gets answers it can grep.
The endpoint is development-only and does nothing in a build.

## Lint

`eslint-plugin-solid` ships two configs for Solid 2.0.
`eslint-plugin-solid/configs/v2`, which the templates enable, switches the version-aware rules to 2.0 semantics and turns on the 2.0-specific rules as errors: `removed-api`, `no-single-arg-create-effect`, `no-accessor-as-prop`, `no-store-mutation-outside-setter`, `no-write-in-pure-computation`, and the server function rules.
`eslint-plugin-solid/configs/v2-strict` adds `no-module-scope-reactive-primitive` and `no-restated-default-options` as errors and promotes the warnings of `v2` to errors.
Each of those rules names a mistake an assistant makes often, so running the linter after an edit reports it before the code runs.
The templates wire the config through oxlint:

```ts
// oxlint.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "oxlint";
import solidV2 from "eslint-plugin-solid/configs/v2";

export default defineConfig({
	jsPlugins: ["eslint-plugin-solid"],
	settings: solidV2.settings,
	rules: solidV2.rules,
});
```

## These docs as Markdown

This site serves its content in the forms an assistant can fetch:

* [`/llms.txt`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/llms.txt) is an index of every page with its one-line description.
* [`/llms-full.txt`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/llms-full.txt) is the whole site in one Markdown file.
* Every page is available as Markdown at its own URL with `.md` appended, for example `/concepts/reactivity.md`.

Give an assistant the index and let it fetch the pages it needs; the full corpus is for tools that load everything once.

## Rules to paste into an instructions file

Drop this block into the project's `AGENTS.md`, which Codex, Cursor, Copilot and Gemini CLI read directly and Claude Code reads when there is no `CLAUDE.md`, and keep it next to the project's own conventions.
It holds the three rules that account for most generated bugs, the names that no longer exist, and pointers to the files above.

```md
## Solid 2.0

This project uses Solid 2.0 (`solid-js` 2.x with `@solidjs/web`). Components run once;
there is no re-render. Read `node_modules/solid-js/CHEATSHEET.md` before writing Solid code,
especially its last section, "What changed from 1.x".

Rules that matter most:

- Props are read, never destructured: `props.name` inside JSX, a memo, or an effect.
  `function Comp({ name })` loses reactivity. Pass values, not accessors: `<Child count={count()} />`.
- `createEffect(compute, apply)` takes two functions. The first reads reactive values and
  returns a result; the second receives it and performs side effects. One argument is an error.
- Stores are written through the draft: `setStore(s => { s.user.name = "Ada" })`.
  There are no path setters and no `produce`.
- Read reactive values inside JSX, a memo, or an effect, never at the top of a component body.
- Do not write a signal or store from a memo, an effect's compute function, or a component body.
  Write from event handlers, `onSettled`, or actions.

Names that no longer exist, and what to use:

- `solid-js/web` -> `@solidjs/web`; `solid-js/store` -> `solid-js`
- `Suspense` -> `Loading`; `SuspenseList` -> `Reveal`; `ErrorBoundary` -> `Errored`
- `mergeProps` -> `merge`; `splitProps` -> `omit`; `unwrap` -> `snapshot`; `onMount` -> `onSettled`
- `createResource` -> an async `createMemo` or `createStore(fn)` read under `<Loading>`
- `createSelector` -> `createProjection`; `createComputed` -> `createMemo` or a two-function `createEffect`
- `batch` -> writes batch on a microtask (`flush()` applies them now); `on()` -> the compute half of `createEffect`
- `startTransition` / `useTransition` -> built in; `isPending()` reports an in-flight change
- `Index` -> `<For keyed={false}>`; `indexArray` -> `mapArray`; `createMutable` -> `createStore` with draft setters
- `onError` / `catchError` -> `<Errored>` or the `error` option of `createEffect`
- `classList` -> `class={{ active: isActive() }}`; `use:` directives -> `ref={factory(args)}`
- `Context.Provider` -> `<Context value={...}>`; `equalFn` -> `isEqual`; `getListener` -> `getObserver`

Tooling:

- Skills: `node_modules/solid-js/skills/solid-2.0/SKILL.md` (primer),
  `node_modules/solid-js/skills/reactivity-diagnostics/SKILL.md` (every warning code and its fix),
  `node_modules/@solidjs/diagnostics/skills/agent-loops/SKILL.md` (capture evidence, assert budgets),
  `node_modules/@solidjs/web/skills/server-components/SKILL.md` (server components and slots).
- A console warning with a bracketed code, such as `[REACTIVE_WRITE_IN_OWNED_SCOPE]`, is a defect.
  Look it up in the repair guide; do not suppress it.
- Verify a reactive change with `captureArtifact` and `expectNoDiagnostics` from `@solidjs/diagnostics`,
  or `POST /__solid/diagnostics` on the dev server with `{"method":"begin"}` ... `{"method":"end"}`.
- Lint with `eslint-plugin-solid/configs/v2` (or `v2-strict`).
- Docs: https://v2.solidjs.com/llms.txt; append `.md` to any page URL for its Markdown.
```

Every name in the block is checked against the installed cheatsheet; when the cheatsheet and this page disagree, the cheatsheet matches your version.

## Recap

* The cheatsheet, four skills, and the template's `AGENTS.md` are installed with the packages, so they match the version in `node_modules`.
* A development build reports structural mistakes with a stable code and a footer that names the repair guide; every code is a defect.
* `captureArtifact` with `expectNoDiagnostics` and `expectRerunBudget` turns a reactive claim into evidence a test or an assistant can check.
* With `diagnostics: true`, `POST /__solid/diagnostics` drives `begin`, `end`, `active`, `whyDidRun`, and `costs` against the running page.
* `eslint-plugin-solid/configs/v2` catches destructured props and the other common generated mistakes before the code runs.
* `/llms.txt`, `/llms-full.txt`, and every page's `.md` URL serve these docs as Markdown.
* Paste the rules block into the assistant's instructions file and keep the project's own conventions beside it.

## Next steps

* [Debugging reactivity](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/guides/debugging-reactivity): how to read a diagnostic report and the test matchers that fail on one.
* [Thinking in Solid](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/guides/thinking-in-solid): the mental model the rules above come from, built up over one feature.
* [Streaming AI responses](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/building-apps/server-functions/streaming-ai-responses): forward a model's stream through a server function into a store, with cancellation.
* [Chat state for the AI SDK](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/guides/ai-sdk-chat): a store-backed adapter for the AI SDK's chat class.

# Chat state for the AI SDK

Source: https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/guides/ai-sdk-chat.md

You have an API route that answers `POST /api/chat` with `streamText(...).toUIMessageStreamResponse()` from the `ai` package, and you want the chat screen in Solid.
The package's own framework adapters hold messages in their framework's state, and `@ai-sdk/solid` is deprecated: its README says so, names AI SDK 5 as the release that removes it, and its last version stops at the `useChat` hook of that era.

Nothing in the chat logic depends on a framework, though.
`AbstractChat` in `ai` does the transport, the stream parsing, tool calls, and status; it reads and writes its messages through a small `ChatState` interface that the adapter supplies.
This recipe is that adapter on a Solid store, about sixty lines, with no throttle, because a store update already touches only the nodes that read the changed value.

This recipe targets `ai` 7.x; the interface is quoted from its source.
Install the package with your package manager, no `@ai-sdk/*` UI package is needed.

## The interface to implement

`ChatState` has seven members:

```ts
export interface ChatState<UI_MESSAGE extends UIMessage> {
	status: ChatStatus;
	error: Error | undefined;
	messages: UI_MESSAGE[];
	pushMessage: (message: UI_MESSAGE) => void;
	popMessage: () => void;
	replaceMessage: (index: number, message: UI_MESSAGE) => void;
	snapshot: <T>(thing: T) => T;
}
```

`AbstractChat` sets `status` and `error` as the request moves through `submitted`, `streaming`, `ready`, and `error`, reads `messages` to build the next request, and writes through `pushMessage`, `popMessage`, and `replaceMessage` as chunks arrive.
`snapshot` must return a copy it can mutate: the stream processor keeps one working message object and hands it to `replaceMessage` after every chunk.

## The adapter

```ts
// src/lib/chat.ts
import {
	AbstractChat,
	type ChatInit,
	type ChatState,
	type ChatStatus,
	type UIMessage,
} from "ai";
import { createSignal, createStore, reconcile, snapshot } from "solid-js";

class SolidChatState<M extends UIMessage> implements ChatState<M> {
	#messages = createStore<M[]>([]);
	#status = createSignal<ChatStatus>("ready");
	#error = createSignal<Error | undefined>();

	constructor(initial: M[] = []) {
		this.messages = initial;
	}

	get status() {
		return this.#status[0]();
	}
	set status(value: ChatStatus) {
		this.#status[1](value);
	}

	get error() {
		return this.#error[0]();
	}
	set error(value: Error | undefined) {
		this.#error[1](value);
	}

	get messages() {
		return this.#messages[0];
	}
	set messages(value: M[]) {
		this.#messages[1](reconcile(value.map((m) => this.snapshot(m))));
	}

	pushMessage = (message: M) => {
		this.#messages[1]((draft) => {
			draft.push(this.snapshot(message));
		});
	};

	popMessage = () => {
		this.#messages[1]((draft) => {
			draft.pop();
		});
	};

	replaceMessage = (index: number, message: M) => {
		const copy = this.snapshot(message);
		this.#messages[1](
			reconcile(this.messages.map((m, i) => (i === index ? copy : m)))
		);
	};

	snapshot<T>(thing: T): T {
		return structuredClone(snapshot(thing));
	}
}

export class Chat<M extends UIMessage = UIMessage> extends AbstractChat<M> {
	constructor({ messages, ...init }: ChatInit<M> = {}) {
		super({ ...init, state: new SolidChatState<M>(messages) });
	}
}
```

Three decisions in that file are worth knowing about.

`status` and `error` are signals and `messages` is a store, so a component that reads `chat.status` re-runs only when the status changes, and a component that reads one message's text re-runs only when that text changes.
The stream processor calls `replaceMessage` once per chunk with a message whose last text part has grown.
Assigning that object into the array slot would replace the row and re-run every reader of it, so the adapter passes the array through [`reconcile`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/stores/reconcile) instead: rows match by `id` and keep their proxies, the unchanged rows are skipped by reference, and inside the changed row only the `text` leaf that differs notifies its readers.

`pushMessage` and `popMessage` write the draft directly, because adding and removing a row is what `push` and `pop` do on a store without touching the other rows.

`snapshot` copies twice on purpose.
Solid's [`snapshot`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/advanced/store-advanced/snapshot) turns a store proxy into plain data, which `structuredClone` can then copy; a plain object passes through the first call unchanged and is copied by the second.
The copy matters in `replaceMessage` as much as in `snapshot`: the stream processor goes on mutating the message object it handed over, and a store that adopted that same object as its backing would see the data change underneath it with no write to track.

:::note[No throttle]
The framework adapters that ship with the AI SDK accept a `throttleWaitMs` that batches message updates for a view that re-renders on each one.
A Solid store update is per key, so there is no view to re-render and nothing to throttle.
If a model produces chunks faster than the screen can paint, the writes are already batched to a microtask.
:::

## Use it in a component

```tsx
// src/pages/Support.tsx
import { For, Show } from "solid-js";
import { DefaultChatTransport, type UIMessage } from "ai";
import { Chat } from "../lib/chat";

function text(part: UIMessage["parts"][number]) {
	return part.type === "text" ? part.text : "";
}

function Support() {
	const chat = new Chat({
		transport: new DefaultChatTransport({ api: "/api/chat" }),
	});

	return (
		<>
			<ul>
				<For each={chat.messages} keyed={(message) => message.id}>
					{(message) => (
						<li>
							<b>{message().role}</b>
							<For each={message().parts}>
								{(part) => <span>{text(part)}</span>}
							</For>
						</li>
					)}
				</For>
			</ul>
			<form
				onSubmit={(event) => {
					event.preventDefault();
					const input = event.currentTarget.elements.namedItem(
						"text"
					) as HTMLInputElement;
					chat.sendMessage({ text: input.value });
					input.value = "";
				}}
			>
				<input name="text" disabled={chat.status !== "ready"} />
				<button type="submit">Send</button>
				<button
					type="button"
					disabled={chat.status !== "streaming"}
					onClick={() => chat.stop()}
				>
					Stop
				</button>
			</form>
			<Show when={chat.error}>
				{(error) => <p role="alert">{error().message}</p>}
			</Show>
		</>
	);
}
```

Type a question and send it.
The user message appears, the input disables while `status` is `submitted` and then `streaming`, and the assistant's reply fills in as the stream arrives; press Stop and the reply keeps what has landed, and `status` returns to `ready`.

`chat.messages` is the store, so the `For` reads it as a reactive list; keyed by `id`, a message's `li` survives every chunk, and only the `span` whose part text changed updates.
`text(part)` is called inside the JSX expression, so the read of `part.text` is tracked there; reading it at the top of the callback would freeze it at the first chunk.
`chat.status` and `chat.error` read the signals through the getters on `AbstractChat`, which is why `disabled` and the error paragraph follow them.

The `Chat` instance is created in the component body, which gives its signals and store an owner, so they are disposed with the component.

## The server side

The route is the AI SDK's own and has nothing Solid-specific in it; this is the shape that [API routes](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/building-apps/middleware-and-api-routes#api-routes) take with the filesystem router:

```ts
// src/routes/api/chat.ts
import type { APIHandler } from "filesystem-routing/api";
import { convertToModelMessages, streamText, type UIMessage } from "ai";

export const POST: APIHandler = async ({ request }) => {
	const { messages }: { messages: UIMessage[] } = await request.json();
	const result = streamText({
		model: provider("your-model"),
		messages: await convertToModelMessages(messages),
		abortSignal: request.signal,
	});
	return result.toUIMessageStreamResponse();
};
```

`provider` is a stand-in for the model provider package you install.
Passing `request.signal` as `abortSignal` is the same cancellation contract as in [Streaming AI responses](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/building-apps/server-functions/streaming-ai-responses#the-cancellation-contract): `chat.stop()` aborts the fetch, the request's signal fires on the server, and the model call stops.

## What you give up

`AbstractChat` reads and writes every message through the adapter, so the adapter is the whole integration, but the chat is not a Solid computation.
It does not participate in a `Loading` boundary, `isPending` does not report its requests, and a navigation during a stream does not hold the frame; `status` is the only progress signal.
For a chat that must take part in the page's async coordination, read the stream through a projection as the streaming guide does, and use the AI SDK only on the server.

## Recap

* `AbstractChat` from `ai` 7.x takes a `ChatState` with `status`, `error`, `messages`, `pushMessage`, `popMessage`, `replaceMessage`, and `snapshot`.
* Hold `status` and `error` in signals and `messages` in a store; push and pop on the draft, and replace through `reconcile` so rows keep their identity.
* `snapshot` returns a copy, and `replaceMessage` stores a copy too, because the stream processor keeps mutating the object it hands over.
* No throttle: a store write touches only the nodes that read the changed key.
* Create the `Chat` in the component body so its reactive state has an owner.
* `@ai-sdk/solid` is deprecated; this adapter replaces it.

## Next steps

* [Streaming AI responses](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/building-apps/server-functions/streaming-ai-responses): the same stream as a projection, with the cancellation contract spelled out.
* [Stores](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/concepts/stores): drafts, `snapshot`, and why a keyed list keeps its rows.
* [Middleware and API routes](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/building-apps/middleware-and-api-routes): where the `/api/chat` route lives and what the handler receives.

# From Solid 1.x

Source: https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/migration/from-solid-1.md

Solid 2 changes the execution model as well as the API names.
Plan the migration as an application-level upgrade, then convert one subsystem at a time.

## Migration order and compatibility boundary

Upgrade the runtime, renderer, JSX compiler, and framework integrations together.
Solid 2 does not provide the old `solid-js/web` or `solid-js/store` package exports, and `@solidjs/web` requires Solid 2 as a peer.
A library that imports removed paths or depends on Solid 1 effect, store, or resource behavior needs a Solid 2-compatible release.

Use this order:

1. Create a migration branch and record the passing Solid 1 test, client-build, and server-render baselines.
2. Upgrade `solid-js`, the renderer package, the Vite plugin (`@solidjs/vite-plugin` replaces `vite-plugin-solid`), and framework adapters as one dependency set.
3. Move imports and JSX types until TypeScript and the production build resolve the new package boundary.
4. Convert setter timing, effects, lifecycle code, and writes inside reactive scopes.
5. Convert stores and store utilities.
6. Replace resources, removed transition APIs, mutations, and async boundaries.
7. Update client rendering, server-side rendering (SSR), hydration, and host integrations.
8. Run tests in development mode to expose Solid 2 diagnostics, then verify production client and server builds.

Do not use a passing type check as proof that an integration is compatible.
Compiler transforms, root event delegation, hydration IDs, and async scheduling are runtime contracts.

## Move packages and JSX ownership

Web rendering and web JSX types moved out of `solid-js`.
Store APIs moved in the other direction and are now exported from `solid-js`.

```ts
// Solid 1
import { createStore, reconcile } from "solid-js/store";
import { hydrate, render } from "solid-js/web";

// Solid 2
import { createStore, reconcile } from "solid-js";
import { hydrate, render } from "@solidjs/web";
```

Update web projects to use the renderer as the JSX type owner:

```json
{
	"compilerOptions": {
		"jsx": "preserve",
		"jsxImportSource": "@solidjs/web"
	}
}
```

Import DOM-specific `JSX` and `ComponentProps` types from `@solidjs/web`.
Use renderer-neutral types such as `Component` and `Element` from `solid-js` when an API does not depend on DOM JSX.

The alternate renderers also moved:

* `solid-js/h` moved to `@solidjs/h`.
* `solid-js/html` moved to `@solidjs/html`.
* `solid-js/universal` moved to `@solidjs/universal`.
* `solid-js/jsx-runtime` and `solid-js/jsx-dev-runtime` moved to renderer-owned entries such as `@solidjs/web/jsx-runtime`.

Search source files, generated code, test configuration, package export maps, and declaration files for the old paths.

## Convert signals and staged writes

The getter and setter pair from [`createSignal`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/reactivity/create-signal) remains.
Setter visibility changed.
Solid 2 stages ordinary writes and commits the reactive queue on the next microtask.
A read immediately after a setter returns the last committed value.

```ts
const [count, setCount] = createSignal(0);

setCount(1);
count(); // 0

flush();
count(); // 1
```

Most event handlers need no explicit flush.
Add [`flush()`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/reactivity/flush) only at an imperative boundary that must observe updated reactive state or DOM before the next microtask.
Tests are a common example.
`flush(fn)` runs the writes in a synchronous flush scope and drains the queue before it returns.

Remove `batch`.
Consecutive writes already share the default microtask batch.
Replacing each `batch` call with `flush` would change deferred work into synchronous work.

Development mode also rejects writes in ordinary owned scopes such as component bodies and memo computations.
Replace write-back derivations with [`createMemo`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/reactivity/create-memo), and invoke setters from event handlers, actions, or effect effect functions.
Reserve `ownedWrite: true` for an internal signal that intentionally accepts in-scope writes.

Solid 2 warns when a component body reads a reactive value at top level because the read is outside a tracking scope.
Keep reactive props and store properties inside JSX expressions or computations.
Use [`untrack`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/reactivity/untrack) only for an intentional one-time read.

```tsx
// Solid 1 code that loses reactivity in Solid 2
function Heading({ title }: { title: string }) {
	return <h1>{title}</h1>;
}

// Solid 2
function Heading(props: { title: string }) {
	return <h1>{props.title}</h1>;
}
```

Function-form `createSignal(fn)` is new.
It creates a writable derived signal and can replace a derivation that previously wrote back into another signal.

## Split effects into compute and effect phases

[`createEffect`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/reactivity/create-effect) now separates dependency tracking from the side effect:

```ts
// Solid 1
createEffect(() => {
	document.title = title();
});

// Solid 2
createEffect(
	() => title(),
	(value) => {
		document.title = value;
	}
);
```

The compute function tracks reactive reads and must remain free of application writes.
The effect function is untracked, may perform imperative work, and may return a cleanup function.
Extract store properties in the compute phase instead of passing a store proxy through and reading it in the untracked effect phase.

```ts
createEffect(
	() => ({ name: user.name, role: user.role }),
	(value) => sendAnalytics(value.name, value.role)
);
```

Return effect cleanup from the effect function:

```ts
createEffect(
	() => roomId(),
	(id) => {
		const connection = connect(id);
		return () => connection.close();
	}
);
```

The Solid 1 `initialValue` argument is removed from `createEffect` and `createMemo`.
The compute function receives `prev`, which is `undefined` on its first run.
Use a default parameter when the computation needs a first previous value.
The second `createMemo` argument is now its options object.

Replace common lifecycle and effect helpers as follows:

* Replace `on(...)` with the compute function and use the effect `defer` option when needed.
* Replace `onMount` with [`onSettled`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/lifecycle-actions/on-settled) and return cleanup from its callback.
* Replace effect-local `onCleanup` calls with cleanup returned from the effect function.
* Use `createTrackedEffect` only when one tracked callback is required.
  It and `onSettled` cannot create nested primitives.
* Replace `catchError` or `onError` with an [`Errored`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/components-jsx/errored) boundary or the effect bundle `error` callback.

## Convert stores to draft setters

[`createStore`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/stores/create-store) still returns a read-only store and its setter.
The setter now receives a mutable draft.
This preserves the property-level model from Solid 1 while making draft mutation the default update form.

```ts
// Solid 1
setState("user", "address", "city", "Paris");

// Solid 2
setState((draft) => {
	draft.user.address.city = "Paris";
});
```

Delete `produce(...)` wrappers and pass the producer body directly to the setter.
Replace `createMutable` and `modifyMutable` with `createStore` and explicit draft setters.
Store writes follow the same staged-write timing as signals.

The setter takes no path arguments.
A Solid 1 path setter becomes a draft write to the same path; ranges and filters become ordinary loops, and setting `undefined` to remove a key becomes `delete`:

```ts
// Solid 1: setState("items", { from: 1, to: 4, by: 2 }, 99)
setState((draft) => {
	for (let i = 1; i <= 4; i += 2) draft.items[i] = 99;
});

// Solid 1: setState("todos", (todo) => todo.done, "archived", true)
setState((draft) => {
	for (const todo of draft.todos) if (todo.done) todo.archived = true;
});

// Solid 1: setState("nickname", undefined)
setState((draft) => {
	delete draft.nickname;
});
```

`reconcile` now runs against the selected draft:

```ts
// Solid 1
setState("todos", reconcile(serverTodos));

// Solid 2
setState((draft) => {
	reconcile(serverTodos, "id")(draft.todos);
});
```

Review these utility changes:

* Replace `unwrap(store)` with [`snapshot(store)`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/advanced/store-advanced/snapshot) when serialization or external code needs a plain non-reactive value.
* Replace `mergeProps` with [`merge`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/stores/merge).
  `undefined` is an explicit overriding value in `merge`.
* Replace `splitProps(props, ["a", "b"])` with [`omit(props, "a", "b")`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/stores/omit).
* Replace selector-shaped state with [`createProjection`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/stores/create-projection) or function-form `createStore`.

Use [`deep(store)`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/advanced/store-advanced/deep) in an effect compute phase when the effect must subscribe to every nested property.
Use `snapshot(store)` when the effect needs the current plain value without subscribing to the store.

## Replace resources with async computations

Solid 2 computations accept promises and async iterables.
Replace a basic `createResource` with an async memo:

```ts
// Solid 1
const [user] = createResource(userId, fetchUser);

// Solid 2
const user = createMemo(() => fetchUser(userId()));
```

Place reads that can be initially unresolved under [`Loading`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/components-jsx/loading):

```tsx
<Loading fallback={<UserSkeleton />}>
	<UserProfile user={user()} />
</Loading>
```

This is the primary first-load model.
The boundary owns branch readiness and renders its fallback until the required reads settle.
After content has rendered, a later update is held and keeps the committed content visible.

:::caution[Async computations change when the screen updates]
A write to an input of an async computation is held until that computation has its next answer, and everything else in the same update waits with it.
Solid 1 resources and effect-based fetching never did this; each consumer updated on its own schedule.
An application that converts all of its fetching at once inherits the new behavior everywhere, and a shared input such as a period selector then waits for the slowest fetch that reads it.
[Data fetching from Solid 1](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/migration/data-fetching-from-solid-1) shows how to keep each pattern working unchanged first, then convert one fetch at a time and choose the refetch behavior per fetch.
:::

The properties and actions on a Solid 1 resource become separate operations:

* Replace `resource.loading` with a `Loading` boundary for initial readiness and [`isPending(() => resource())`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/reactivity/is-pending) for an in-flight changed answer.
* Replace `resource.error` with an `Errored` boundary or an effect `error` callback.
* Replace `refetch()` with [`refresh(resource)`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/lifecycle-actions/refresh).
* Replace `mutate()` with an action and [`createOptimistic`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/reactivity/create-optimistic) or [`createOptimisticStore`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/stores/create-optimistic-store).
* Replace `resource.latest` with [`latest(resource)`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/reactivity/latest) when imperative code must inspect an in-flight value.

A bare `refresh()` re-asks the same question without making `isPending` true.
If the refresh must present as pending, call [`affects(target)`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/lifecycle-actions/affects) in the surrounding action before `refresh(target)`.
Use a mutation-specific optimistic flag when the UI needs to show the progress of the mutation itself.

`loadingValue` and the store option `seedLoadingValue` declare a placeholder that answers for the source before its first result.
Use them when provisional data should render through the same UI as the final data, or when a Solid 1 `undefined` check must stay in the JSX.
The declared value prevents first-flight suspension and keeps `isPending` false until the first real answer arrives.
Use `Loading` when provisional data cannot truthfully have the final value's shape.

## Convert mutations and remove transition APIs

Remove `startTransition` and `useTransition`.
Solid 2 coordinates async computations through the graph.
Use `Loading` for unresolved branches, `isPending` for an unrevealed changed answer, and optimistic primitives for tentative mutation state.

[`action`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/lifecycle-actions/action) is for imperative workflows whose writes cross an async gap.
An action is a generator or async generator and returns a promise.
Writes to ordinary signals and stores remain held by the transaction, while optimistic writes are visible and revert to their derived or base value when the transaction settles.

```ts
const [todos, setTodos] = createOptimisticStore(fetchTodos, []);

const addTodo = action(function* (todo: Todo) {
	setTodos((draft) => {
		draft.push(todo);
	});
	yield saveTodo(todo);
	refresh(todos);
});
```

Yield promises to preserve the action transaction.
If an async generator uses `await` for a typed result, add a bare `yield` before later writes to re-enter the transaction.
Do not call `flush()` inside an action because it drains the transaction step.
Invoke actions from event handlers or another imperative scope, not from a component or computation body.

Read more about the unified model in [Async reactivity](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/concepts/async-reactivity).

## Update boundaries, control flow, and JSX

Apply these direct UI migrations:

* Replace `Suspense` with `Loading`.
* Replace `ErrorBoundary` with `Errored`.
  Its function fallback receives an error accessor, so read the error with `error()`.
* Replace `SuspenseList` with [`Reveal`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/components-jsx/reveal).
* Replace `Index` with [`For keyed={false}`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/components-jsx/for).
  The item is an accessor and the index is a stable number in this mode.
* Replace `Context.Provider` with the context component: `<Theme value={value}>`.
* Replace `<Dynamic component={source} {...props} />` with a component from [`dynamic()`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-web/components/dynamic): `const Comp = dynamic(() => source)`, then `<Comp {...props} />`.
  `Dynamic` is deprecated.
  Create the component once, outside the JSX, and render it wherever it is needed; a falsy source renders nothing, as before.
* Replace direct `createDynamic(source, props)` calls with `dynamic(source)`.
* Use [`dynamicComponent`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-web/components/dynamic) from `solid-js` instead when the source only ever answers with a component, never a tag name; it does not keep the element runtime in the bundle.

Update removed JSX forms:

* Replace `classList` with the object or array form of `class`.
* Replace `use:directive` with a `ref` callback or directive factory, and use a `ref` array to compose callbacks.
* Replace `on:` and `oncapture:` with camel-case Solid event props.
  Use a `ref` callback and `addEventListener` when native listener options are required.
* Rename lowercase handlers such as `onclick={fn}` to `onClick`.
  Only `on` followed by an uppercase letter is an event handler; a lowercase `onclick` or a leftover `on:click` compiles to a plain attribute without an error, and development warns `[LOWERCASE_EVENT_ATTRIBUTE]` when it receives a function.
* Replace `attr:` and `bool:` with standard attributes and boolean presence.
* Remove `/*@once*/`.
  Keep values reactive, use DOM default properties such as `defaultValue` for initial state, or take a narrow JavaScript snapshot with `untrack`.

Rendering into nested roots, `ShadowRoot` instances, or portals needs integration testing.
Solid 2 scopes delegated events to each render root and disposes those listeners with the root.
Remove calls to the old document-global `clearDelegatedEvents` API.

## Update client rendering and SSR

Import [`render`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-web/rendering-ssr/render), [`hydrate`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-web/rendering-ssr/hydrate), and all server render functions from `@solidjs/web`.
Continue to retain and call the dispose function returned by `render`.

Choose the SSR entry point by the required result:

* [`renderToString`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-web/rendering-ssr/render-to-string) is synchronous and renders `Loading` fallbacks for unresolved reads.
* [`renderToStream`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-web/rendering-ssr/render-to-stream) emits the shell and then resolved async fragments.
* Replace `renderToStringAsync` with `await renderToStream(() => <App />)` when a fully settled HTML string is required.
* Use exactly one stream consumer: `pipe`, `pipeTo`, or `readable`.
  The `readable` stream contains `Uint8Array` chunks and can be passed to a web `Response`.

Review the `ssrSource` and `deferStream` options on every migrated resource.
The default `ssrSource: "server"` adopts the serialized server result without repeating the initial client computation.
Use `"hybrid"` or `"client"` only when the computation has verified client-specific behavior.

Code that owns the HTTP exchange is an integration boundary.
Solid 2 exposes request events, response-head helpers, server functions, and stream response utilities through `@solidjs/web`, but routing, middleware policy, sessions, and deployment adapters still need framework-specific migration work.
Do not infer replacements for those APIs from similar names.
Follow the integration's Solid 2 guide and verify its request, response, hydration, and serialization tests.

## Replace removed APIs by intent

The following list covers common application APIs and is not a complete export-diff table.
Choose replacements by behavior:

* `createComputed`: use `createMemo` for a derived value, split `createEffect` for a side effect, or function-form `createSignal` for writable derived state.
* `batch`: rely on default batching; use `flush` only for synchronous observation.
* `on`: put dependencies in the effect compute phase.
* `onMount`: use `onSettled`.
* `onError` and `catchError`: use `Errored` or an effect `error` callback.
* `createResource`: use async computations and boundaries.
* `createMutable` and `modifyMutable`: use `createStore` and draft setters.
* `produce`: pass its draft callback directly to the store setter.
* `createSelector`: use `createProjection` or function-form `createStore`.
* `from` and `observable`: use async iterables for inbound streams or a split effect for outbound notifications.
  A standard Observable adapter has no direct core replacement.
* `createDeferred`: move the scheduling policy outside Solid.
* `indexArray`: use `mapArray` with `{ keyed: false }`.
* `resetErrorBoundaries`: remove it; error boundaries recover through their current graph state or explicit reset callback.
* `enableScheduling` and `writeSignal`: remove internal or obsolete usage.

Audit undocumented imports separately.
An export that existed for compiler, renderer, devtools, or metaframework integration may have no application-level replacement.
Treat those imports as host-integration work and confirm them against the owning package source.

## Update tests

Update test compilation to use the renderer's JSX runtime.
For web component tests, resolve the browser and development package conditions so tests exercise `@solidjs/web` rather than the server entry.
Keep Testing Library cleanup or call render disposers explicitly.

Account for staged writes in unit tests:

```ts
setCount(2);
flush();
expect(count()).toBe(2);
```

Flush after effect creation before asserting the effect function.
Flush after setters before asserting reactive values, effects, or DOM.
Prefer `await user.click(...)` for user-level tests because event tooling also drains its event sequence.

Use [`resolve(() => value())`](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/reference/solid-js/advanced/interop-async/resolve) when a test must wait for a reactive expression to settle.
Await action calls before asserting their final committed or reverted state.
Test the initial `Loading` fallback, the settled content, the held-update pending state, and error boundary as separate states.

Run migration tests in development mode.
Fix top-level reactive-read warnings, writes from owned scopes, actions called from computations, and async reads outside a `Loading` boundary instead of suppressing the diagnostics.
Then run the same client, SSR, streaming, and hydration paths in production mode.

See the [Testing guide](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/guides/testing) for the current test environment split.

## Final verification

Before merging the migration:

1. Search for old package paths and removed symbols.
2. Run TypeScript, lint, and the production client build.
3. Run unit and component tests with explicit flush points.
4. Exercise initial load, a changed-input update, manual refresh, successful mutation, failed mutation, and boundary recovery.
5. Compare SSR shell output, streamed completion, hydration, and event behavior with the recorded Solid 1 baseline.
6. Verify each third-party primitive, renderer, router, and metaframework package against an explicit Solid 2-compatible release.

## Next steps

* [Data fetching from Solid 1](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/migration/data-fetching-from-solid-1): convert resource and effect-based fetching one fetch at a time and choose the refetch behavior for each.
* [From SolidStart](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/migration/from-solid-start), [From Solid Router](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/migration/from-solid-router), and [From Solid Meta](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/migration/from-solid-meta): the framework-level migrations that build on this one.
* [Async reactivity](https://v2-rebuild--solid-docs-v2.netlify.app/concepts/async-reactivity): the model behind held updates, `Loading`, `isPending`, and actions.
